Main.sentence: Cocaine is a central nervous system ___E:stimulant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stimulant)___ and ___E:tropane alkaloid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropane_alkaloid)___ derived primarily from the leaves of two ___E:coca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca)___ species native to South America: Erythroxylum coca and E. novogranatense .

Coca leaves are processed into ___E:cocaine paste U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine_paste)___ , a crude mix of ___E:coca alkaloids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca_alkaloids)___ from which cocaine base is isolated and converted to cocaine hydrochloride , commonly known as "cocaine".

Cocaine was once a standard ___E:topical medication U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topical_medication)___ as a ___E:local anesthetic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_anesthetic)___ with intrinsic ___E:vasoconstrictor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasoconstriction)___ activity, but its high abuse potential, adverse effects, and cost have limited its use and led to its replacement by other medicines.    "Cocaine and its combinations" are formally excluded from the ___E:WHO Model List of Essential Medicines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WHO_Model_List_of_Essential_Medicines)___ .

Street cocaine is commonly ___E:snorted U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_administration)___ , ___E:injected U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injection_(medicine))___ , or smoked as ___E:crack cocaine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crack_cocaine)___ , with effects lasting up to 90 minutes depending on the route.

Cocaine acts pharmacologically as a ___E:serotonin–norepinephrine–dopamine reuptake inhibitor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serotonin%E2%80%93norepinephrine%E2%80%93dopamine_reuptake_inhibitor)___ (SNDRI),    producing reinforcing effects such as ___E:euphoria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphoria)___ , increased ___E:alertness U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alertness)___ , ___E:concentration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attentional_control)___ , ___E:libido U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphrodisiac)___ , and reduced fatigue and ___E:appetite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anorectic)___ .
Cocaine has numerous ___E:adverse effects U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adverse_effect)___ .

Acute use can cause ___E:vasoconstriction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasoconstriction)___ , ___E:tachycardia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tachycardia)___ , ___E:hypertension U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertension)___ , ___E:hyperthermia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperthermia)___ , seizures, while overdose may lead to ___E:stroke U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke)___ , ___E:heart attack U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myocardial_infarction)___ , or ___E:sudden cardiac death U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudden_cardiac_death)___ .

Cocaine also produces a spectrum of ___E:psychiatric symptoms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatric_symptoms)___ including agitation, paranoia, anxiety, irritability, ___E:stimulant psychosis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stimulant_psychosis)___ , hallucinations, delusions, violence, as well as ___E:suicidal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicidal_ideation)___ and homicidal thinking.   ___E:Prenatal exposure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prenatal_cocaine_exposure)___ poses risks to fetal development.

Chronic use may result in ___E:cocaine dependence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine_dependence)___ , withdrawal symptoms, ___E:neurotoxicity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurotoxicity)___ , and ___E:nasal damage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org#Cocaine_nose)___ , including ___E:cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine-induced_midline_destructive_lesions)___ .
No approved medication exists for cocaine dependence, so psychosocial treatment is primary.

Cocaine is frequently ___E:laced U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacing_(drugs))___ with ___E:levamisole U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levamisole)___ to increase bulk.   This is linked to ___E:vasculitis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasculitis)___ ( CLIV ) and ___E:autoimmune U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoimmunity)___ conditions ( CLAAS ).

Coca cultivation and its subsequent processes occur primarily ___E:Latin America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America)___ , especially in the ___E:Andes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes)___ of Bolivia, Peru, and Colombia, though cultivation is expanding into ___E:Central America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America)___ , including Honduras, Guatemala, and Belize.

Violence linked to the cocaine trade continues to affect ___E:Latin America and the Caribbean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America_and_the_Caribbean)___ and is expanding into ___E:Western Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe)___ , ___E:Asia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia)___ , and ___E:Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa)___ as ___E:transnational organized crime U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transnational_organized_crime)___ groups compete globally.
Cocaine remains the world's fastest-growing ___E:illicit drug market U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illegal_drug_trade)___ .
Coca chewing dates back at least 8,000 years in South America.

Large-scale cultivation occurred in ___E:Taiwan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan)___ and ___E:Java U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java)___ prior to ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ .

Decades later, the ___E:cocaine boom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine_boom)___ marked a sharp rise in illegal cocaine production and trade, beginning in the late 1970s and peaking in the 1980s.

Cocaine is regulated under ___E:international drug control conventions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_drug_control_conventions)___ , though ___E:national laws vary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_status_of_cocaine)___ : several countries have decriminalized small quantities.
Coca leaves have been used by ___E:Andean civilizations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andean_civilizations)___ since ___E:ancient times U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andean_civilizations)___ .

In ancient ___E:Wari culture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wari_culture)___ ,  ___E:Inca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_people)___ culture, and through modern successor ___E:indigenous U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples)___ cultures of the ___E:Andes Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes_Mountains)___ , coca leaves are chewed, taken orally in the form of a ___E:tea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca_tea)___ , or alternatively, prepared in a sachet wrapped around alkaline burnt ashes, and held in the ___E:mouth against the inner cheek U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buccal_pouch)___ ; it has traditionally been used as an ___E:anorectic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anorectic)___ and to combat the effects of cold and ___E:altitude sickness U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude_sickness)___ ,   although its actual effectiveness has never been systematically studied.
Globally, in 2019, cocaine was used by an estimated 20 million people (0.4% of adults aged 15 to 64 years).

The highest prevalence of cocaine use was in ___E:Australia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia)___ and ___E:New Zealand U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand)___ (2.1%), followed by ___E:North America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America)___ (2.1%), ___E:Western U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe)___ and ___E:Central Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Europe)___ (1.4%), and ___E:South U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America)___ and ___E:Central America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America)___ (1.0%).

Since 1961, the ___E:Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_Convention_on_Narcotic_Drugs)___ has required countries to make recreational use of cocaine a ___E:crime U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime)___ .

In the United States, cocaine is regulated as a ___E:Schedule II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schedule_II_Controlled_Substance)___ drug under the ___E:Controlled Substances Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Controlled_Substances_Act)___ , meaning that it has a high potential for abuse but has an accepted medical use.  While rarely used medically today, its accepted uses include serving as a topical local anesthetic for the upper ___E:respiratory tract U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_tract)___ and as an ___E:antihemorrhagic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antihemorrhagic)___ agent to stop bleeding in the mouth, throat, and nasal cavities.

It is legal for people to use ___E:coca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca)___ leaves in the ___E:Andean Community U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andean_Community)___ , such as ___E:Peru U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru)___ and ___E:Bolivia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia)___ , where they are chewed, consumed in the form of tea, or are sometimes incorporated into food products.

Coca leaves are typically mixed with an alkaline substance (such as ___E:slaked lime U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium_hydroxide)___ ) and chewed into a wad that is retained in the ___E:buccal pouch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buccal_pouch)___ (mouth between gum and cheek, much the same as ___E:chewing tobacco U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chewing_tobacco)___ is chewed) and sucked of its juices.

The juices are absorbed slowly by the ___E:mucous membrane U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mucous_membrane)___ of the inner cheek and by the ___E:gastrointestinal tract U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastrointestinal_tract)___ when swallowed.

Coca herbal ___E:infusion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infusion)___ (also referred to as ___E:coca tea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca_tea)___ ) is used in coca-leaf producing countries much as any herbal medicinal infusion would elsewhere in the world.

The free and legal commercialization of dried coca leaves under the form of filtration bags to be used as "coca tea" has been actively promoted by the governments of ___E:Peru U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru)___ and ___E:Bolivia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia)___ for many years as a drink having ___E:medicinal powers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_medicine)___ .

In Peru, the ___E:National Coca Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Coca_Company)___ , a state-run corporation, sells cocaine-infused teas and other medicinal products and also exports leaves to the U.S. for medicinal use.  The effects of drinking coca tea are mild stimulation and mood lift.

In 1986 an article in the Journal of the American Medical Association revealed that U.S. ___E:health food stores U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_food_store)___ were selling dried coca leaves to be prepared as an infusion as "Health Inca Tea".
While the packaging claimed it had been "decocainized", no such process had actually taken place.

The article stated that drinking two cups of the tea per day gave a mild ___E:stimulation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stimulation)___ , increased ___E:heart rate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_rate)___ , and ___E:mood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotional_mood)___ elevation, and the tea was essentially harmless.

___E:Ypadú U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ypadu)___ or ypadu (also known as mambé) is an unrefined, unconcentrated ___E:powder U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powder_(substance))___ made from toasted ___E:coca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca)___ leaves and the ash of various other plants.
It is traditionally prepared and consumed by indigenous tribes in the Northwest Amazon.

Like coca teas consumed in ___E:Peru U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru)___ to adapt to sickness induced by high elevation, it has a long ___E:ethnobotanical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnobotanical)___ history and cultural associations.

___E:Karl Koller U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Koller_(ophthalmologist))___ 's groundbreaking discovery of cocaine as a local anesthetic is regarded as the second most significant advance in the history of anesthesia.
Although cocaine was once widely preferred for topical anesthesia, the search for replacement agents intensified due to rising costs, strict regulations, and its habit-forming potential.

Cocaine is not included on the ___E:WHO Model List of Essential Medicines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WHO_Model_List_of_Essential_Medicines)___ ; the list formally excludes "cocaine and its combinations" as therapeutic alternatives to ___E:ophthalmological preparations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WHO_Model_List_of_Essential_Medicines#Ophthalmological_preparations)___ .

Today, the US ___E:Drug Enforcement Administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_Enforcement_Administration)___ (DEA) classifies cocaine as a ___E:Schedule II drug U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schedule_II_drug)___ , recognizing its high potential for abuse but still permitting its limited use for medical purposes.

However, current ___E:pharmacoepidemiological U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmacoepidemiology)___ trends suggest that cocaine may soon reach the point where, in practical terms, it is no longer used medically in health care as a Schedule II substance.
This report may prompt some states (such as North Dakota) and institutions to reconsider whether further efforts to identify alternative agents are needed.
As physician boards—but not pharmacy boards—continue to assess knowledge of licit cocaine, attention may shift toward drugs with more contemporary medical use.

Cocaine is rarely prescribed in modern medicine due to its high potential for abuse and significant risk of adverse effects; its use is now almost exclusively limited to ___E:health facilities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_facility)___ for specific diagnostic procedures or surgeries.
Cocaine is used in medical practice as a ___E:topical medication U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topical_medication)___ .
Because it is not absorbed into the bloodstream in significant amounts when used this way, topical application does not produce the psychoactive effects associated with recreational cocaine use.

Cocaine is sometimes used in ___E:otorhinolaryngology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otorhinolaryngology)___ as a ___E:topical anesthetic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topical_anesthetic)___ and ___E:vasoconstrictor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasoconstrictor)___ to help control pain and bleeding during surgery of the nose, mouth, throat, or ___E:lacrimal duct U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacrimal_duct)___ .

It is also used for topical airway anaesthesia for procedures such as awake fibreoptic ___E:bronchoscopy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronchoscopy)___ or ___E:intubation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intubation)___ .

Although some absorption and systemic effects may occur, the use of cocaine as a topical anesthetic and vasoconstrictor is generally safe, rarely causing ___E:cardiovascular U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiovascular)___ toxicity, ___E:glaucoma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucoma)___ , and ___E:pupil dilation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mydriasis)___ .

Occasionally, cocaine is mixed with ___E:adrenaline U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrenaline)___ and ___E:sodium bicarbonate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_bicarbonate)___ and used topically for surgery, a formulation called ___E:Moffett's solution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moffett%27s_solution)___ .

It is occasionally used in surgeries involving the ___E:pharynx U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharynx)___ or ___E:nasopharynx U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasopharynx)___ to reduce pain, bleeding, and ___E:vocal cord spasm U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laryngospasm)___ .

Nasal solution cocaine hydrochloride ( Goprelto ), an ester used for intranasal application, was approved for medical use in the United States in December 2017, and is indicated for the introduction of topical anesthesia of the mucous membranes for diagnostic procedures and surgeries on or through the nasal cavities of adults.

Cocaine hydrochloride ( Numbrino ) was approved for medical use in the United States in January 2020.   Headache and ___E:epistaxis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistaxis)___ are the most frequently reported adverse reactions with Goprelto,  while hypertension and tachycardia-including ___E:sinus tachycardia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinus_tachycardia)___ -are most common with Numbrino.

Cocaine ___E:eye drops U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_drop)___ have traditionally been used by ___E:neurologists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurology)___ when examining people suspected of having ___E:Horner syndrome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horner%27s_syndrome)___ .
In Horner syndrome, ___E:sympathetic innervation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sympathetic_innervation)___ to the eye is blocked.

In a healthy eye, cocaine stimulates the ___E:sympathetic nervous system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sympathetic_nervous_system)___ (SNS) by inhibiting norepinephrine reuptake, causing the ___E:pupil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pupil)___ to dilate.

In patients with Horner syndrome, sympathetic innervation to the eye is disrupted, so the affected pupil does not dilate in response to cocaine and remains constricted, or dilates to a lesser extent than the unaffected eye, which also receives the eye drop test. If both eyes dilate equally, the patient does not have Horner syndrome.

However, ___E:apraclonidine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apraclonidine)___ has largely replaced cocaine as the first-line pharmacologic agent for the diagnosis of Horner syndrome in routine clinical practice.

Recreational cocaine is typically not taken by mouth due to its poor bioavailability, instead it is usually ___E:snorted U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_administration)___ or ___E:injected U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injection_(medicine))___ .

Cocaine hydrochloride can also be chemically converted into its ___E:free base U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_base)___ form, ___E:crack cocaine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crack_cocaine)___ , which can be vaporized.
Cocaine is a ___E:central nervous system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_nervous_system)___ ___E:stimulant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stimulant)___ .
Its effects can last from 15 minutes to an hour. The duration of cocaine's effects depends on the amount taken and the route of administration.

Cocaine can be in the form of fine white powder and has a bitter taste. ___E:Crack cocaine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crack_cocaine)___ is a smokeable form of cocaine made into small "rocks" by processing cocaine with ___E:sodium bicarbonate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_bicarbonate)___ (baking soda) and water.

Cocaine use leads to increases in alertness, feelings of well-being and ___E:euphoria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphoria)___ , increased energy and ___E:motor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor_control)___ activity, and increased feelings of competence and ___E:sexuality U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_sexuality)___ .

Expectations about cocaine's effects—both positive and negative—can influence how people feel after using it. Surprisingly, expecting negative effects may increase the drug's perceived positive impact, making quitting or avoiding cocaine more difficult for some individuals.

Analysis of the ___E:correlation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation_and_dependence)___ between the use of 18 various ___E:psychoactive substances U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychoactive_substance)___ shows that cocaine use correlates with other " ___E:party drugs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_drug)___ " (such as ___E:MDMA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MDMA)___ or ___E:amphetamines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphetamines)___ ), as well as with ___E:heroin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heroin)___ and ___E:benzodiazepines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benzodiazepine)___ use, and can be considered as a bridge between the use of different groups of drugs.

Nasal ___E:insufflation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insufflation_(medicine))___ (known colloquially as "snorting", "sniffing", or "blowing") is a common method of ingestion of recreational powdered cocaine.
The drug coats and is absorbed through the mucous membranes lining the ___E:nasal passages U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_passages)___ .
Cocaine's desired euphoric effects are delayed when snorted through the nose by about five minutes.

This occurs because cocaine's absorption is slowed by its constricting effect on the blood vessels of the nose.  Insufflation of cocaine also leads to the longest duration of its effects (60–90 minutes).
When insufflating cocaine, absorption through the nasal membranes is approximately 30–60%
In a study of cocaine users, the average time taken to reach peak subjective effects was 14.6 minutes.

Any damage to the inside of the nose is due to cocaine constricting blood vessels—and therefore restricting blood and oxygen/nutrient flow—to that area, which, after chronic use, may cause " ___E:cocaine nose U:(https://en.wikipedia.org#Cocaine_nose)___ ."
Most ___E:banknotes have traces of cocaine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contaminated_currency)___ on them; this has been confirmed by studies done in several countries.

In 1994, the ___E:U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Ninth_Circuit)___ cited findings that in Los Angeles, three out of four banknotes were tainted by cocaine or another illicit drug.

___E:Snuff spoons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snuff_spoon)___ , hollowed-out ___E:pens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pen)___ , cut ___E:straws U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drinking_straw)___ , pointed ends of keys,  long ___E:fingernails U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingernails)___ or ___E:artificial nails U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_nails)___ , and (clean) ___E:tampon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampon)___ applicators are also used to insufflate cocaine.

The cocaine typically is poured onto a flat, hard surface (such as a mobile phone screen, ___E:plate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_(dishware))___ , mirror, CD case or book) and divided into "bumps", "lines" or "rails", and then insufflated.
A 2001 study reported that the sharing of straws used to "snort" cocaine can spread blood diseases such as ___E:hepatitis C U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepatitis_C)___ .
Historically, ___E:snuff spoons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snuff_spoon)___ were used for cocaine in the 20th century, hence the names "cocaine spoon" and "coke spoon".

Some local statutes in the US treat spoons that are too small and thus "unsuited for the typical, lawful uses of a spoon" as ___E:drug paraphernalia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_paraphernalia)___ .

Subjective effects not commonly shared with other methods of administration include a ringing in the ears moments after injection (usually when over 120 milligrams) lasting 2 to 5 minutes including ___E:tinnitus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinnitus)___ and audio distortion.
This is colloquially referred to as a "bell ringer".
In a study of cocaine users, the average time taken to reach peak subjective effects was 3.1 minutes.
The euphoria passes quickly.

Aside from the toxic effects of cocaine, there is also the danger of circulatory ___E:emboli U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embolism)___ from the insoluble substances that may be used to cut the drug. As with all injected ___E:illicit substances U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illicit_substances)___ , there is a risk of the user contracting ___E:blood-borne infections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood-borne_disease)___ if sterile injecting equipment is not available or used.

___E:Coca paste U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca_paste)___ (paco, basuco, oxi, pasta) is a crude ___E:extract U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extract)___ of the ___E:coca leaf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca_leaf)___ which contains 40% to 91% ___E:cocaine freebase U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine_freebase)___ along with companion coca alkaloids and varying quantities of ___E:benzoic acid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benzoic_acid)___ , ___E:methanol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methanol)___ , and ___E:kerosene U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerosene)___ .
The caustic reactions associated with the local application of coca paste prevents its use by oral, intranasal, mucosal, intramuscular, intravenous or subcutaneous routes.
Coca paste can only be smoked when combined with a combustible material such as tobacco or cannabis.

Crude cocaine preparation intermediates are marketed as cheaper alternatives to pure cocaine to local markets while the more expensive end product is exported to United States and European markets. ___E:Freebase cocaine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freebase_cocaine)___ paste preparations can be smoked.
The psychological and physiological effects of the paco are quite severe.
Media usually report that it is extremely toxic and addictive.
According to a study by Intercambios, media appear to exaggerate the effects of paco .
These stereotypes create a sense that nothing can be done to help a paco addict and thus stand in the way of rehabilitation programs.
Powder cocaine (cocaine hydrochloride) must be heated to a high temperature to be smoked (about 197 °C), and considerable decomposition/burning occurs at these high temperatures.
This effectively destroys some of the cocaine and yields a sharp, acrid, and foul-tasting smoke.
Cocaine base/crack can be smoked because it vaporizes with little or no decomposition at 98 °C (208 °F),  which is below the boiling point of water.
Cocaine should not be used in individuals with a known allergy or ___E:hypersensitivity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersensitivity)___ to the drug or any components of its topical formulation.

It is also contraindicated in ___E:elderly patients U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geriatrics)___ and those with a history of hypertension or ___E:cardiovascular disease U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiovascular_disease)___ .
___E:Prenatal cocaine exposure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prenatal_cocaine_exposure)___ (PCE) may occur when a pregnant woman uses cocaine.

Under the former FDA ___E:pregnancy category U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pregnancy_category)___ system, cocaine was classified as a Category C drug. Its potential to cause harm to the fetus is not fully known, so it should only be administered to pregnant women if clearly necessary.
Cocaine can act as a ___E:teratogen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teratogen)___ , having various effects on the developing fetus.

Some common teratogenic defects caused by cocaine include ___E:hydronephrosis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydronephrosis)___ , ___E:cleft palate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleft_lip_and_cleft_palate)___ , ___E:polydactyly U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polydactyly)___ , and ___E:down syndrome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_syndrome)___ .

Cocaine as a drug has a low molecular weight and high water and lipid solubility which enables it to cross the ___E:placenta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Placenta)___ and fetal blood-brain barrier.
Because cocaine is able to pass through the placenta and enter the fetus, the fetus' circulation can be negatively affected.

With restriction of fetal circulation, the development of organs in the fetus can be impacted, even resulting in ___E:intestines developing outside U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastroschisis)___ of the fetus' body.  Cocaine use during pregnancy can also result in ___E:obstetric labor complications U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obstetric_labor_complication)___ such as, ___E:placental abruption U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Placental_abruption)___ ,  ___E:preterm birth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preterm_birth)___ or delivery, ___E:uterine rupture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uterine_rupture)___ , ___E:miscarriage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miscarriage)___ , and ___E:stillbirth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stillbirth)___ .

Chronic intranasal usage can degrade the ___E:cartilage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartilage)___ separating the ___E:nostrils U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nostrils)___ (the ___E:septum nasi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septum_nasi)___ ), leading eventually to its complete disappearance.
The cause of "cocaine nose" can be traced to the chemical process that occurs when cocaine hydrochloride is insufflated (snorted).

As cocaine is absorbed through the ___E:nasal mucosa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_mucosa)___ , the remaining hydrochloride component forms a dilute ___E:hydrochloric acid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrochloric_acid)___ .
The short half-life of cocaine,  combined with binge use, may expose the nasal tissues to this acidic environment more frequently, increasing the risk of irritation and damage.
For people with cocaine abuse, mild symptoms may resolve completely with total abstinence from cocaine, making early involvement of addiction services essential.

Repair may involve ___E:rhinoplasty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhinoplasty)___ , which includes creating a new internal lining with nasolabial flaps and restoring support with costal cartilage grafts.

In 2024, Belgian doctors report a rise in patients needing nose reconstruction due to cocaine use, which damages nasal tissue and cartilage; however, few undergo surgery because it requires at least six months of abstinence from cocaine for proper healing.

Some individuals seek ___E:plastic surgery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic_surgery)___ to repair or reconstruct nasal damage caused by cocaine use, although surgical outcomes can be complicated by ongoing tissue loss and poor healing.

When nasal damage is too severe for reconstruction, a ___E:nose prosthesis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nose_prosthesis)___ may be used to restore appearance and ___E:quality of life U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality_of_life)___ .
According to the ___E:European Union Drugs Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union_Drugs_Agency)___ , the estimated minimum lethal dose is 1.2 grams.

However, sensitive individuals have died from as little as 30 milligrams applied to mucous membranes-an amount that is 40 times less than the minimum lethal dose. In contrast, addicts may tolerate doses as high as 5 grams per day.
Cocaine can be snorted, swallowed, injected, or smoked.
Most deaths due to cocaine are accidental but may also be the result of ___E:body packing or stuffing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mule_(smuggling))___ with rupture in the gastrointestinal tract.

Alcohol impairment increases the likelihood of risk-taking behaviors and susceptibility to ___E:peer pressure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer_pressure)___ , and also raises the risk of overdose due to the formation of ___E:cocaethylene U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaethylene)___ (see the ___E:alcohol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org#Alcohol)___ section).

Use of cocaine causes ___E:abnormally fast heart rhythms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiac_arrhythmia)___ and a marked elevation of blood pressure ( ___E:hypertension U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertension)___ ), which can be life-threatening.

This can lead to death from acute ___E:myocardial infarction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myocardial_infarction)___ , acute ___E:respiratory failure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_failure)___ (i.e., ___E:hypoxemia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypoxemia)___ , with or without ___E:hypercapnia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercapnia)___ ), ___E:stroke U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke)___ , ___E:cerebral hemorrhage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerebral_hemorrhage)___ , and ___E:sudden cardiac arrest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiac_arrest)___ .

Overdose can also cause acute ___E:hepatotoxicity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepatotoxicity)___ —typically due to toxic metabolites—though most cases resolve quickly; however, fatal outcomes from ___E:multiple organ dysfunction syndrome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_organ_dysfunction_syndrome)___ are possible, and there is no specific antidote.
Cocaine overdose may result in ___E:hyperthermia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperthermia)___ as stimulation and increased muscular activity cause greater heat production.
Heat loss is also inhibited by the cocaine-induced ___E:vasoconstriction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasoconstriction)___ .

In 2024, drug-related deaths in England and Wales reached their highest level in three decades, with a notable increase in fatalities involving cocaine and experts urging urgent government intervention to address the crisis.

Martin Powell, from the charity Transform, which campaigns for the ___E:legal regulation of drugs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_liberalization)___ , suggested that the recent rise in cocaine-related deaths in the UK may be due to the increased purity of cocaine, leading users to consume it more frequently and alongside other substances.

___E:Alcohol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_(drug))___ interacts with cocaine in vivo to produce ___E:cocaethylene U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaethylene)___ , another psychoactive substance which may be substantially more ___E:cardiotoxic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiotoxic)___ than either cocaine or alcohol by themselves.

In 2024, a systematic review of human studies concluded that, despite some inconsistencies in the findings, the co-use of cocaine and alcohol poses a significantly greater risk of cardiovascular fatalities compared to cocaine use alone.
This elevated risk is largely attributed to the formation of cocaethylene, a unique and toxic metabolite produced only when both substances are consumed together.

Cocaethylene is associated with an 18- to 25-fold increased risk of sudden death, as well as a higher incidence of myocardial injury and cardiac arrest, underscoring the serious health risks of simultaneous cocaine and alcohol use.

___E:Monoamine oxidase inhibitors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoamine_oxidase_inhibitor)___ (MAOIs) should not be combined with other psychoactive substances (antidepressants, painkillers, stimulants, including prescribed, OTC and illegally acquired drugs, etc.) except under expert care. [citation needed]

The ___E:opioid epidemic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opioid_epidemic)___ now involves more overdose deaths with both opioids and cocaine, especially among non-Hispanic Blacks who are twice as likely to die from combined opioid-stimulant overdoses compared to non-Hispanic whites.
Cocaine-related deaths in Blacks are similar to opioid deaths in whites.
Risk factors include young age, education, urban living, mental disorders, and stress.
It remains unclear if co-use is intentional.
Recent studies expand focus beyond heroin to all opioids, reflecting changing overdose patterns.
The extent of absorption of cocaine into the ___E:circulatory system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circulatory_system)___ after nasal insufflation is similar to that after oral ingestion.
The rate of absorption after nasal insufflation is limited by cocaine-induced vasoconstriction of capillaries in the nasal mucosa.

Onset of absorption after oral ingestion is delayed because cocaine is a weak base with a ___E:pKa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PKa)___ of 8.6, and is thus in an ionized form that is poorly absorbed from the ___E:gastric acid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastric_acid)___ and easily absorbed from the alkaline ___E:duodenum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duodenum)___ .

The rate and extent of absorption from inhalation of cocaine is similar or greater than with intravenous injection, as inhalation provides access directly to the ___E:capillary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capillary)___ bed. The delay in absorption after oral ingestion may account for the popular belief that cocaine bioavailability from the stomach is lower than after insufflation.
Compared with ingestion, the faster absorption of insufflated cocaine results in quicker attainment of maximum drug effects.
Snorting cocaine produces maximum physiological effects within 40 minutes and maximum psychotropic effects within 20 minutes.
Physiological and psychotropic effects from nasally insufflated cocaine are sustained for approximately 40–60 minutes after the peak effects are attained.

Cocaine crosses the ___E:blood–brain barrier U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood%E2%80%93brain_barrier)___ via both a proton-coupled ___E:organic cation antiporter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_cation_transport_protein)___   and (to a lesser extent) via ___E:passive diffusion across cell membranes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passive_transport)___ .
As of September 2022, the gene or genes encoding the human proton-organic cation antiporter had not been identified.

Cocaine has a short elimination half-life of 0.7–1.5 hours and is extensively ___E:metabolized U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolism)___ by ___E:plasma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_plasma)___ esterases and also by liver ___E:cholinesterases U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholinesterase)___ , with only about 1% excreted unchanged in the urine.

The metabolism is dominated by ___E:hydrolytic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrolysis)___ ___E:ester U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ester)___ cleavage, so the eliminated metabolites consist mostly of ___E:benzoylecgonine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benzoylecgonine)___ (BE), the major ___E:metabolite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolite)___ , and other metabolites in lesser amounts such as ecgonine methyl ester (EME) and ___E:ecgonine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecgonine)___ .

Further minor metabolites of cocaine include ___E:norcocaine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norcocaine)___ , p-hydroxycocaine, m-hydroxycocaine, p-hydroxybenzoylecgonine (pOHBE), and m-hydroxybenzoylecgonine.

Depending on ___E:liver U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liver)___ and ___E:kidney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidney)___ functions, cocaine metabolites are detectable in urine between three and eight days. Generally speaking ___E:benzoylecgonine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benzoylecgonine)___ is eliminated from someone's urine between three and five days. In urine from heavy cocaine users, benzoylecgonine can be detected within four hours after intake and in concentrations greater than 150 ng/mL for up to eight days later.

Cocaine and its major metabolites may be quantified in blood, plasma, or urine to monitor for use, confirm a diagnosis of poisoning, or assist in the forensic investigation of a traffic or other criminal violation or sudden death.

Most commercial cocaine ___E:immunoassay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunoassay)___ screening tests cross-react appreciably with the major cocaine metabolites, but ___E:chromatographic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromatography)___ techniques can easily distinguish and separately measure each of these substances.

When interpreting the results of a test, it is important to consider the cocaine usage history of the individual, since a chronic user can develop tolerance to doses that would incapacitate a cocaine-naive individual, and the chronic user often has high baseline values of the metabolites in his system.
Cautious interpretation of testing results may allow a distinction between passive or active usage, and between smoking versus other routes of administration.

___E:Hair analysis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hair_analysis)___ can detect cocaine ___E:metabolites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolite)___ in regular users until after the sections of hair grown during the period of cocaine use are cut or fall out.
Cocaine acts as a ___E:serotonin–norepinephrine–dopamine reuptake inhibitor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serotonin%E2%80%93norepinephrine%E2%80%93dopamine_reuptake_inhibitor)___ (SNDRI).

Cocaine increases levels of ___E:serotonin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serotonin)___ , ___E:norepinephrine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norepinephrine)___ , and ___E:dopamine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopamine)___ in the synaptic cleft, leading to heightened post-synaptic activation, with dopamine contributing to euphoria and arousal, and the other monoamines enhancing additional effects.

The ___E:pharmacodynamics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmacodynamics)___ of cocaine involve the complex relationships of neurotransmitters (inhibiting ___E:monoamine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoamine)___ uptake in rats with ratios of about: ___E:serotonin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5HT)___ :dopamine = 2:3, serotonin: ___E:norepinephrine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norepinephrine)___ = 2:5).

The most extensively studied effect of cocaine on the ___E:central nervous system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_nervous_system)___ is the blockade of the ___E:dopamine transporter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopamine_transporter)___ protein.

Dopamine ___E:neurotransmitter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurotransmitter)___ released during neural signaling is normally recycled via the transporter; i.e., the transporter binds the transmitter and pumps it out of the synaptic cleft back into the ___E:presynaptic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presynaptic)___ ___E:neuron U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuron)___ , where it is taken up into storage ___E:vesicles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vesicle_(biology))___ .
Cocaine binds tightly at the dopamine transporter forming a complex that blocks the transporter's function.

The dopamine transporter can no longer perform its reuptake function, and thus ___E:dopamine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopamine)___ accumulates in the ___E:synaptic cleft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synaptic_cleft)___ .

The increased concentration of dopamine in the synapse activates post-synaptic dopamine receptors, which makes the drug ___E:rewarding U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reward_system)___ and promotes the compulsive use of cocaine.

Cocaine affects certain serotonin (5-HT) receptors; in particular, it has been shown to ___E:antagonize U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receptor_antagonist)___ the ___E:5-HT3 receptor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5-HT3_receptor)___ , which is a ___E:ligand-gated ion channel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligand-gated_ion_channel)___ .
An overabundance of 5-HT 3 receptors is reported in cocaine-conditioned rats, though 5-HT 3 's role is unclear.

The ___E:5-HT2 receptor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5-HT2_receptor)___ (particularly the subtypes ___E:5-HT2A U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5-HT2A_receptor)___ , ___E:5-HT2B U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5-HT2B_receptor)___ and ___E:5-HT2C U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5-HT2C_receptor)___ ) are involved in the ___E:locomotor-activating U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locomotor_activity)___ effects of cocaine.
Cocaine has been demonstrated to bind as to directly stabilize the ___E:DAT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopamine_transporter)___ transporter on the open outward-facing conformation.

Further, cocaine binds in such a way as to inhibit a ___E:hydrogen bond U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_bond)___ innate to DAT. Cocaine's binding properties are such that it attaches so this hydrogen bond will not form and is blocked from formation due to the tightly locked orientation of the cocaine molecule.

Research studies have suggested that the affinity for the transporter is not what is involved in the habituation of the substance so much as the conformation and binding properties to where and how on the transporter the molecule binds.
Conflicting findings have challenged the widely accepted view that cocaine functions solely as a reuptake inhibitor.
To induce euphoria an intravenous dose of 0.3-0.6 mg/kg of cocaine is required, which blocks 66-70% of DAT in the brain.
Re-administering cocaine beyond this threshold does not significantly increase DAT occupancy but still results in an increase of euphoria which cannot be explained by reuptake inhibition alone.

This discrepancy is not shared with other dopamine reuptake inhibitors like ___E:bupropion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bupropion)___ , ___E:sibutramine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sibutramine)___ , ___E:mazindol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazindol)___ or ___E:tesofensine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesofensine)___ , which have similar or higher potencies than cocaine as dopamine reuptake inhibitors.

Furthermore, a similar response-occupancy discrepancy has been observed with ___E:methylphenidate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methylphenidate)___ , which also stabilizes the dopamine transporter in an open outward-facing conformation.

These findings have evoked a hypothesis that cocaine may also function as a so-called "DAT inverse agonist" or "negative allosteric modifier of DAT" resulting in dopamine ___E:transporter reversal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_transport)___ , and subsequent dopamine release into the synaptic cleft from the axon terminal in a manner similar to but distinct from ___E:amphetamines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphetamine)___ .
___E:Sigma receptors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigma_receptor)___ are affected by cocaine, as cocaine functions as a sigma ligand agonist.
Further specific receptors it has been demonstrated to function on are ___E:NMDA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NMDA)___ and the D 1 dopamine receptor.

Cocaine also blocks ___E:sodium channels U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_channel)___ , thereby interfering with the propagation of ___E:action potentials U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_potential)___ ;   thus, like ___E:lignocaine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lignocaine)___ and ___E:novocaine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novocaine)___ , it acts as a local anesthetic.

It also functions on the binding sites to the dopamine and serotonin ___E:sodium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium)___ dependent transport area as targets as separate mechanisms from its reuptake of those transporters; unique to its local anesthetic value which makes it in a class of functionality different from both its own derived ___E:phenyltropanes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenyltropane)___ analogues which have that removed.

In addition to this, cocaine has some target binding to the site of the ___E:κ-opioid receptor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CE%9A-opioid_receptor)___ .  [unreliable medical source?] Cocaine also causes ___E:vasoconstriction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasoconstriction)___ , thus reducing bleeding during minor surgical procedures.
Recent research points to an important role of circadian mechanisms  and ___E:clock genes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clock_genes)___  in behavioral actions of cocaine.

Cocaine is known to suppress hunger and appetite by increasing co-localization of sigma σ 1 R receptors and ___E:ghrelin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghrelin)___ GHS-R1a ___E:cell surface receptors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_surface_receptor)___ , thereby increasing ghrelin-mediated signaling of satiety  and possibly via other effects on appetitive hormones.
Cocaine effects, further, are shown to be potentiated for the user when used in conjunction with new surroundings and stimuli, and otherwise novel environs.
In its purest form, cocaine is a white, pearly powder.
As a ___E:tropane alkaloid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropane_alkaloid)___ , cocaine is a weak base and readily forms salts when combined with acids.
The most commonly encountered form is the hydrochloride (HCl) salt, although other salts such as the sulfate (SO 4 2− ) and nitrate (NO 3 − ) are occasionally observed.
The solubility of these salts varies depending on their polarity; the hydrochloride salt is polar and highly soluble in water.

The first ___E:structure elucidation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_structure#Structural_elucidation)___ and ___E:total synthesis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_synthesis)___ of the cocaine molecule was accomplished by ___E:Richard Willstätter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Willst%C3%A4tter)___ in 1898.  Willstätter's synthesis involved constructing the cocaine structure from simpler precursors, notably via the intermediate ___E:tropinone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropinone)___ .

Subsequent significant contributions to understanding the synthetic pathway and stereochemistry were made by ___E:Robert Robinson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Robinson_(organic_chemist))___ and Edward Leete.

Cocaine contains four ___E:chiral U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiral)___ centers (1 R , 2 R , 3 S , and 5 S ), two of which are ___E:configurationally U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_configuration)___ dependent, resulting in eight possible ___E:stereoisomers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereoisomer)___ .
The formation of inactive stereoisomers, along with various synthetic by-products, limits both the yield and purity of the final product.

Although the chemical synthesis of cocaine is technically feasible, it is generally considered impractical due to its high cost, low efficiency, and challenges in stereoselective synthesis compared to extraction from natural plant sources.

While domestic clandestine laboratories could theoretically reduce reliance on offshore production and international smuggling—as seen with illicit ___E:methamphetamine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methamphetamine)___ —manufacture and synthetic production of cocaine remains rare. Large-scale commercial synthesis has not been explored.

The ___E:biosynthesis of cocaine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biosynthesis_of_cocaine)___ is the natural metabolic process by which the ___E:coca plant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca_plant)___ ( Erythroxylum species) produces cocaine, a ___E:tropane alkaloid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropane_alkaloid)___ , through a multi-step enzymatically catalyzed pathway beginning with ___E:ornithine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornithine)___ or ___E:arginine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arginine)___ and culminating in the formation of the cocaine metabolite ___E:benzoylecgonine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benzoylecgonine)___ .
Large-scale biosynthesis of cocaine is unexplored.
The biosynthesis of cocaine has long attracted the attention of biochemists and organic chemists.

This interest is partly motivated by the strong physiological effects of cocaine, but a further incentive was the unusual ___E:bicyclic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicyclic_molecule)___ structure of the molecule.
The biosynthesis can be viewed as occurring in two phases, one phase leading to the N-methylpyrrolinium ring, which is preserved in the final product.
The second phase incorporates a C4 unit with formation of the bicyclic ___E:tropane U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropane)___ core.
In 2022, a ___E:GMO U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GMO)___ produced N. benthamiana were discovered that were able to produce 25% of the amount of cocaine found in a coca plant.
However, since N. benthamiana also naturally contains ___E:nicotine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotine)___ , separating the cocaine from nicotine and related alkaloids would be challenging.

___E:Personal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_data)___ cards-including ID cards and driver's licenses-are frequently swabbed by inspectors to detect drug residue, as these items are commonly used to prepare lines of cocaine.
Swabbing can reveal traces of cocaine or other illicit substances, providing evidence of recent drug handling or use. This practice may be employed during security checks at border crossings.

A Newsbeat investigation found that "cocaine torches" used by UK police to detect cocaine use are ineffective on typical street cocaine, as independent lab tests showed they fail to make the drug ___E:fluoresce U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluoresce)___ .
Experts and drug charities criticized the devices, warning they can give false positives and waste resources, while police forces defended their use as a deterrent.
The manufacturer says the torches only work on much purer forms of cocaine than are found on the street.
Cocaine may be detected by law enforcement using the ___E:Scott reagent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_reagent)___ .
The test can easily generate ___E:false positives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_positives_and_false_negatives)___ for common substances and must be confirmed with a laboratory test.

Approximate cocaine purity can be determined using 1 mL 2% cupric sulfate pentahydrate in dilute HCl, 1 mL 2% potassium thiocyanate and 2 mL of ___E:chloroform U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloroform)___ .
The shade of brown shown by the chloroform is proportional to the cocaine content.

This test is not cross sensitive to heroin, methamphetamine, ___E:benzocaine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benzocaine)___ , procaine and a number of other drugs but other chemicals could cause false positives.

Both the ___E:pharmaceutical supply chain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine_and_society#Pharmaceutical_supply_chain)___ and the ___E:illicit supply chain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine_and_society#Illicit_supply_chain)___ obtain cocaine from coca cultivated in Latin America, but they operate under very different controls and oversight.

In Peru, for example, legal coca cultivation is monopolized by the state company ___E:National Coca Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Coca_Company)___ (ENACO), yet approximately 90% of coca leaves produced in the country are diverted to illegal actors for cocaine manufacturing.
As a result, these illicit coca crops are a primary target of ongoing government-led ___E:coca eradication U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca_eradication)___ efforts.

Cocaine is prohibited in competition for athletes by the ___E:World Anti-Doping Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Anti-Doping_Agency)___ (WADA), which lists it as a stimulant on its ___E:International Standard for the Prohibited List U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_drugs_banned_by_the_World_Anti-Doping_Agency)___ .  : 6
Cocaine is sometimes referred to on the street as blow, coca, coke, crank, flake, snow, or soda cot. Slang terms for free base cocaine include crack or rock.

___E:Fishscale cocaine U:(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/fishscale#Noun)___ , from fish + scale , is named for its shiny, yellowish flakes that resemble fish scales—distinct from the dull white appearance of standard cocaine powder.

The production, distribution, and sale of cocaine products is restricted (and illegal in most contexts) in most countries as regulated by the ___E:Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_Convention_on_Narcotic_Drugs)___ , and the ___E:United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Convention_Against_Illicit_Traffic_in_Narcotic_Drugs_and_Psychotropic_Substances)___ .

In the United States the manufacture, importation, possession, and distribution of cocaine are additionally regulated by the 1970 ___E:Controlled Substances Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Controlled_Substances_Act)___ .

Some countries, such as Bolivia, Colombia, and Peru, permit the cultivation of coca leaf for traditional consumption by the local ___E:indigenous population U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas)___ , but nevertheless, prohibit the production, sale, and consumption of cocaine.
The provisions as to how much a coca farmer can yield annually is protected by laws such as the Bolivian Cato accord.
In addition, some parts of Europe, the United States, and Australia allow processed cocaine for medicinal uses only.
Cocaine is a Schedule 8 controlled drug in Australia under the ___E:Poisons Standard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_for_the_Uniform_Scheduling_of_Medicines_and_Poisons)___ .
It is the second most popular illicit recreational drug in Australia ___E:behind cannabis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Australia)___ .

In ___E:Western Australia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Australia)___ under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1981, 4.0g of cocaine is the amount of prohibited drugs determining a court of trial, 2.0g is the amount of cocaine required for the presumption of intention to sell or supply, and 28.0g is the amount of cocaine required for purposes of drug trafficking.

The US federal government instituted a national ___E:drug labelling U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prescribing_information)___ requirement for cocaine and cocaine-containing products through the ___E:Pure Food and Drug Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pure_Food_and_Drug_Act)___ of 1906.  : 37 The next important federal regulation was the ___E:Harrison Narcotics Tax Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrison_Narcotics_Tax_Act)___ of 1914. While this act is often seen as the start of prohibition, the act itself was not actually a prohibition on cocaine, but instead it set up a regulatory and licensing regime.

The Harrison Act did not recognize addiction as a treatable condition and therefore the therapeutic use of cocaine, heroin, or morphine to such individuals was outlawed – leading a 1915 editorial in the journal American Medicine to remark that the addict "is denied the medical care he urgently needs, open, above-board sources from which he formerly obtained his drug supply are closed to him, and he is driven to the underworld where he can get his drug, but of course, surreptitiously and in violation of the law." In countries where cocaine is illicitly produced, an intermediate product known as cocaine paste—often referred to as "poor man's cocaine"—is frequently smoked in impoverished communities.
This substance is favored in these areas primarily because it is inexpensive and more accessible than refined cocaine.
However, the use of cocaine paste poses severe health risks.
During its production, various toxic chemicals are used to extract coca alkaloids from the coca leaves.
Many of these hazardous substances, such as solvents and acids, remain in the paste after processing.

When the paste is smoked, individuals are exposed not only to the addictive effects of the drug itself but also to the dangerous residual chemicals, which can cause significant harm to the lungs, nervous system, and overall health.
This combination of affordability, accessibility, and toxicity makes cocaine paste particularly damaging to vulnerable populations in cocaine-producing regions.

The Consolidated Counterdrug Database (CCDB) is a U.S. government dataset created in the 1990s that compiles vetted data on cocaine trafficking and seizures in the ___E:Western Hemisphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Hemisphere)___ "transit zone," involving 26 U.S. agencies and 20 foreign partners.

It provides a highly reliable, conservative record of cocaine movements and interdiction efforts, revealing that despite large seizures, interdiction captures only a small fraction of trafficking events and has minimal impact on U.S. cocaine prices.
The CCDB challenges optimistic views of drug interdiction effectiveness and underscores the need for new policy approaches, yet remains underutilized in research despite being unclassified.
